newsitem.title: UK: UK supermarkets signal no end to petrol price war.
newsitem.headline: UK supermarkets signal no end to petrol price war.

text.p: British supermarkets on Thursday signalled there was no end to the cut-throat petrol price war, exactly one year after Esso launched its Pricewatch campaign.
Tesco Plc, with 265 petrol sites, and ASDA Group Plc, with 122, reiterated their pledges to match the lowest pump prices in their markets.
"There is no way we will roll over and play dead," said Phil Reed, public relations manager at Asda.
"Our position is that we will be consistently low across the board rather than going into short-term price gimmicks and price promotions," he said.
U.K. motorists have enjoyed some of the lowest pump prices in Europe due to the ferocious competition that squeezed margins to as narrow as break-even levels of two pence a litre last summer.
That contributed to a steep rise in petrol site closings and allegations that competition will eventually dry up and lead to higher prices.
The supermarkets, or hypermarkets, have been instrumental in driving down prices by exploiting their lower cost base, some industry analysts said.

"We've also got a price pledge that we made to customers first that we won't be beaten on price," said Karen Marshall, press officer at Tesco, explaining it monitors prices within three miles of its sites.
"We'll continue to make sure we offer the best deal on petrol -- we won't be beaten on price," she said.
Safeway, the supermarket chain owned by Argyll Group Plc with 139 petrol sites, and J. Sainsbury Plc, with 185, were not immediately available for comment.

"I think that when margins move up to about five pence per litre or above, then because the supermarkets have lower costs, they will always be tempted to move down" their prices, said Stephen Brooks, principal consultant at Wood Mackenzie.
Margins did recover at the end of 1996 toward the five pence per litre threshold, he said.
"If (the supermarkets) move and Esso moves to meet them, we will get the spiral down effect that we got at the middle of last year," he said.
Reed said he expected the market to remain "extremely competitive" in 1997 but allegations that supermarkets were selling below cost were untrue.
"We do not sell petrol at a loss," he said.
Supermarkets refused to reveal their market shares.
Brooks has estimated the price war could boost the share held by the hypermarket groups and the top four oil companies to 85 percent by 2000, from 66 pct in 1995.
